opus-5.5.text:
I think the paradigm has to shift from optimizing single responses to optimizing trajectories. In the chatbot era, post-training was mostly about making one answer look good: SFT on high-quality demonstrations, then preference optimization so the model's tone and helpfulness match what humans like. For agents, that's not enough. What matters is whether the model can complete a long task in a real environment: call tools, read feedback, recover from mistakes, and know when it's done.

So in my view, the core of agent post-training should be reinforcement learning in environments with verifiable outcomes. You give the model a real task, like fixing a bug in a repository, finishing a research question, or operating a browser, and you let it explore. The reward should come as much as possible from the environment itself: did the tests pass, was the answer correct, was the goal state reached. Not from a reward model guessing whether something "looks right." Once the reward is grounded in reality, the model can discover strategies we never wrote down for it.

But RL alone doesn't solve everything. I'd describe it in three layers.

First, the base model and mid-training need to already contain agentic priors. If the pretraining or mid-training data has almost no long-horizon tool use, code execution traces, or multi-step reasoning, then RL is just searching in the dark. A small amount of high-quality cold-start data helps the model learn the format and basic behaviors, so exploration starts from a reasonable place.

Second, the biggest bottleneck is actually environments, not algorithms. People talk a lot about GRPO versus PPO and so on, but the real leverage is building a large, diverse set of environments and tasks that are hard enough, verifiable, and not easy to hack. If your environments are narrow, the model overfits to them. If your rewards are leaky, the model will find the leak. A lot of engineering effort should go into scaling environments the way we used to scale pretraining data.

Third, there's the long-horizon problem. When a trajectory is hundreds of steps and tens of thousands of tokens, credit assignment becomes very hard, and the infrastructure, meaning rollout efficiency, asynchronous training, and context management, becomes a first-class research problem. How the model manages its own context, summarizes, and decides what to remember is itself something post-training should teach, not something we hardcode in a scaffold.

So if I had to summarize: agent post-training should be environment-centric, outcome-driven RL on top of a base model that already has agentic priors, with a lot of investment in scaling environments and infrastructure. And I think the boundary between pretraining and post-training will keep blurring. Eventually the model learns by interacting, not just by imitating.

r001.rationale: The response says agent post-training should optimize full trajectories and whether the model completes long tasks in real environments, including using tools, responding to feedback, and reaching the goal state.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I think the core issue is that most post-training today was designed for chat, and agents are not chat. In a chat model, the unit of supervision is one turn: the model says something, a human or a reward model judges it, done. For an agent, the unit is a trajectory. The model might take thirty or fifty actions, call tools, read results, revise its plan, and the thing you actually care about is whether the task got done at the end, not whether any single step looked nice. So the paradigm has to move from turn-level feedback to trajectory-level feedback.

Concretely, I think there are three pieces.

The first is the environment. If you do not have a real environment where the model can act and see consequences, you are just doing imitation learning on human demonstrations, and that ceiling is low. The model copies the surface behavior of a good trajectory but does not learn why those actions were chosen. So you need executable environments: code sandboxes, browsers, simulated APIs, whatever the domain is. And you need many of them, with verifiable outcomes, because that is where the reward comes from. Honestly, I think building environments is now more important than building another SFT dataset.

The second is the reward design. For things like code and math you can get a verifiable signal, tests pass or they do not. That is where reinforcement learning has worked best so far, and I do not think that is a coincidence. The harder question is what you do when the outcome is not cleanly verifiable, like a research task or a long multi-step workflow. My view is you still anchor on outcomes as much as possible, and you use process supervision only to shape behavior you can clearly articulate, like "do not fabricate a tool result" or "check your work before declaring done." If you over-engineer process rewards, the model learns to perform the process rather than solve the problem.

The third piece, which people underrate, is long-horizon credit assignment and exploration. When a trajectory fails at step forty, which of the earlier decisions caused it? Plain outcome RL is very sample inefficient here. So you need the model to be able to reflect, to recover from mistakes mid-trajectory, and you need training signal that rewards recovery, not just clean runs. A good agent is not one that never makes errors, it is one that notices and fixes them. If your training data only contains perfect trajectories, you never teach that.

One more thing I would add: the base model matters more than people admit. A lot of agent capability is really long-context reasoning plus a good world model of tools and systems. If pretraining has not seen enough of that, post-training is fighting uphill. So I would say the right paradigm is pretraining that already exposes the model to tool use and long interaction traces, then SFT mostly as a cold start to get the format and basic behaviors, and then the bulk of the compute going into RL in real environments with outcome-based rewards. The ratio is shifting. Two years ago it was mostly SFT with a bit of RL on top. For agents, I think it inverts.

r001.rationale: The response says agent post-training should focus on whole trajectories and whether the task was completed, including long sequences of tool use and planning.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to move from training a model to produce a good answer to training it to complete a task over a whole trajectory. For an agent, the answer is only one part of the behavior. It also has to decide what information it needs, when to use a tool, how to interpret feedback, and what to do when its first attempt fails.

So I would put interaction with an environment at the center of post-training. You can use demonstrations to establish basic behaviors, then use reinforcement learning on tasks with outcomes you can meaningfully check. Did the agent actually solve the problem? Did it respect the constraints? How much time and how many interactions did it take?

The difficult part is credit assignment. If a task takes fifty steps and fails at the end, which decision should change? You need reliable outcome signals, but also ways to diagnose the trajectory without rewarding superficial patterns, like producing a longer plan or calling more tools.

And I wouldn’t expect one fixed training recipe to be sufficient. The task distribution and the environments need to evolve as the model improves. Otherwise, you risk training an agent that is very good at the training setup but brittle when something unfamiliar happens. For me, the real test is whether it can use feedback to recover and make progress on a new task.

r001.rationale: The response advocates training agents to complete tasks over a whole trajectory and emphasizes interacting with an environment. It does not clearly specify complex tasks within complex agent frameworks as the post-training objective.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to move from training models to produce good answers toward training them to complete tasks. For an agent, the answer is only one part of the process. It also has to decide what information it needs, which tool to use, whether an action worked, and when to change its approach.

So post-training should happen in an interactive environment, with feedback over the whole trajectory. Demonstrations can give the model a useful starting point, but reinforcement learning should let it explore different strategies and learn from the consequences. If we only imitate successful trajectories, we don’t necessarily teach it how to recover when something goes wrong.

The difficult part is designing the environments and rewards. A reward that is easy to measure may encourage behavior that looks successful without actually satisfying the user. We need verifiable outcomes where possible, and we need to evaluate whether the model can transfer what it learns to unfamiliar tasks.

I would also include asking for clarification and knowing when to stop as part of the training objective. A good agent shouldn’t simply take more steps. It should make useful progress, recognize uncertainty, and complete the task with an appropriate amount of effort.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly shifts post-training’s objective from producing answers to completing tasks, and describes learning across the full agent trajectory, including information gathering, tool use, checking outcomes, and adapting. This communicates end-to-end task completion in an agent framework.
